newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Central America broadening trade horizons.
newsitem.headline: Central America broadening trade horizons.

text.p: Central America must look to expand its trade ties to the Caribbean and South America, as it is uncertain whether it will be taken into the fold of the North American Free Trade Agreement, Honduran President Carlos Roberto Reina said on Wednesday.
Central American countries have gradually integrated their economies in recent years, forming joint strategies on trade.
A key component of that is seeking "NAFTA parity," in which Central America would receive similar benefits as Mexico in trade with the United States and Canada.

But in a summit of Central American presidents meeting in Honduras, leaders said they could not count on becoming junior partners in NAFTA, the treaty linking the United States, Canada and Mexico in a trade union.

Above all else, Central America has sought to export textiles to the United States duty free, and although the Clinton administration has said it is sympathetic to the idea, it faces stiff opposition in the U.S. Congress.

"We can't sit down and place our hopes in these kinds of concessions, so as fast as possible we have move closer to the Caribbean and Mercosur (a South American trade bloc) ... in order to improve our economies," Reina told reporters on Wednesday, a day after the summit ended.
The presidents on Tuesday agreed to seek a free-trade agreement with the Caribbean trading bloc CARICOM in 1997.

The small Central American nations of Honduras, Guatemala, El Salvador and Costa Rica have banded together to better compete in the world market, their economies depending largely on agriculture. They are joined by neighbouring Panama, which relies more on financial services and the Panama Canal.

"The decision of the presidents is evidence of their desire to stop playing all their cards with the United States and still improve trade and investment possibilities," said Honduran political analyst Efrain Diaz, a former deputy in the Central American parliament.

But the United States historically is the top trading partner for all of the Central American countries, and Costa Rican President Jose Maria Figueres said on Tuesday that "for our development, the opening of this market (the United States) is vital."
